posts.cooked:
I’m doing a build vs. buy analysis on how to achieve strikethrough pricing on PDPs and Google products, that’s easy to maintain with a small team. Curious which solutions merchants are currently using, not what you plan or hope to do.

I’ve read through many threads about why it’s hard out of the box, and using compare-at price is a hack. I’d like to us native discounts if possible.

Team is 3 people, 1k products, sales on regular basis, significant traffic from google product search, so very common use case.

Current setup:

  • how are you displaying the strikethrough? compare-at price? custom app or scripts?
  • which app are you using, if any?

Tradeoffs:

  • is it more manual than you’d like?
  • is reporting/analytics for how much in discounts you’re giving away?
  • any issues crop up caused by your solution?

Any feedback is helpful.

Hi @PeteJelliffe,

I saw your build-vs-buy analysis for a three-person team managing around 1,000 products, regular sales and significant Google Product traffic.

Did you eventually choose compare-at pricing, native discounts, or a third-party app?

What is still the hardest part today: keeping Shopify and Google prices aligned, verifying the storefront after a campaign, or reporting exactly how much discount was applied?

What I see most with stores your size: compare-at for long markdowns (so Google Shopping picks them up), and scheduled automatic discounts for short sales like BFCM, so nobody has to revert 1000 prices on Monday.

The catch with automatic discounts is they only show in the cart unless your theme or an app displays them on the product page. And Google still sees full price.

If you go compare-at, export a CSV of original prices before every sale. Saves a lot of pain.

(Full disclosure, I work on DiscountEasy, which does the product page part, so take my view with that in mind.)

Good split above: compare-at for longer markdowns, automatic discounts for short promos. The part I’d add is the end of a compare-at sale, because that’s where most pricing mistakes happen: the sale gets reverted by hand or by a bulk edit, and a few variants end up at the wrong price (or still showing a strikethrough) for weeks.

What’s worked for us:

  1. Snapshot before you touch anything. Export products (Products > Export, CSV) right before the sale starts. That file is your only record of the original price and compare-at per variant. Shopify doesn’t keep a price history you can roll back to.
  2. Start and end the sale the same way. If you set sale prices with a CSV import, end it by re-importing the snapshot rather than editing back by hand. Mixed methods (CSV in, manual out) are where variants get missed.
  3. Check three things the day after it ends: filter products where compare-at price is not empty (leftover strikethroughs), spot-check a few variants against the snapshot, and look at Merchant Center diagnostics for price mismatches. Google re-crawls on its own schedule, so a mismatch can show up a day or two later.
  4. For a hard stop on Google, make sure your feed sends the sale price with an effective date range (most feed setups support it). That way Shopping ads stop showing the sale even if a storefront revert runs late.

For a ~1,000-product catalog that’s about 20 minutes per sale, and it saves the “why is this still 30% off?” email three weeks later.

Hi Pete,

For strikethrough on the product page and in Google Shopping, the native path that actually changes what shoppers see is compare-at price, not an automatic discount.

Two built-in options, depending on what you need to show:

  1. Automatic discount with a start and end date (Discounts, then Create discount). Product prices never change, so there is nothing to put back when the sale ends. That is the lower-risk option for a short sale. The catch, which others in this thread already noted, is that many themes only show the discount in the cart, and Google often still receives the regular price.

  2. Compare-at price plus a lower Price, set with Shopify’s bulk editor or a product CSV. Most themes then show the crossed-out price on the product page, and Google can pick up the sale price. Before you change anything, export your products (Products, Export, CSV) and keep that file with the date in the name. Shopify does not keep a price history you can roll back to. When the sale ends, re-import that file (tick “Overwrite products with matching handles”) or undo the same columns in the bulk editor. Anything a colleague or a supplier changes during the sale can be overwritten by that old file, so strip the import down to Handle, variant identifiers, Variant Price, and Variant Compare-at Price.

Shopify Flow can also schedule a price change with a scheduled trigger and a “Send Admin API request” action (productVariantsBulkUpdate). You would still need a second workflow to put prices back, and a place to store the originals, because Flow will not remember them for you.

If you want the compare-at sale to start and end on its own, I built an app for that. Disclosure: I am the developer of AE Bulk Price Editor Sale. You filter the products, preview every change, apply a percent, amount, or fixed price on Price and/or compare-at, and schedule the start and end. It reverts the originals when the sale ends, and you can undo from history. It does not create discount codes. Free covers up to 150 variant updates a month. Standard is $12/month and Premium is $25/month, each with a 14-day trial.

Listing: AE Bulk Price Editor Sale - Schedule a Black Friday sale, then auto-revert originals | Shopify App Store

The automatic discount path is still the one I would try first if a cart-only discount is enough for a short promo. Use compare-at when you need the strikethrough on the product page and in Google, and export first either way.

Amanda

posts.cooked:
For a 3-person team running ~1,000 SKUs with heavy Google Product Search traffic, the main reason most stores still fall back to Compare-at price during promos is Google Merchant Center parity: Shopify’s native Automatic Discounts only apply at cart/checkout unless you customize theme Liquid + metafields, and Google’s crawler expects the discounted price and sale_price directly in the product feed and structured JSON-LD on the PDP.

To keep Compare-at price sales fast and reversible without manual errors or margin surprises:

  1. Export a pre-sale rollback CSV first: Filter Products > Export to your sale collection and save that untouched file as your instant undo button when the promo ends.
  2. Guard margins before uploading: In your staging sheet, calculate the post-promo Variant Price against Cost per item (plus payment fees/shipping) and flag any SKU where Sale Price <= Cost—flat 20–30% discounts frequently push low-margin variants or add-ons underwater silently.
  3. Keep inventory columns out of price CSVs: Delete Variant Inventory Qty from your sale and rollback CSVs so uploading prices never overwrites live stock sold mid-campaign.
  4. Track giveaway without native discount codes: Tag the sale items or log (Compare-at price - Sale price) per SKU at launch so you can multiply against Shopify’s Sales by product report afterward.

I put together a quick 2-minute walkthrough showing how to check discount margins and catch below-cost SKUs before launching a sale: https://youtu.be/mfmnkCQtNn0

Disclosure: I’m the developer of Revise (Revise: Cost, Stock & Bulk - Simulate profit, sync stock & bulk-edit with drift-safe undo. | Shopify App Store, $0 Free forever plan), which lets you preview sale margins and save one-click catalog rollback snapshots—happy to look over an anonymized sample of your SKU/cost sheet at support@unkrypt.com if you’d like.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
For a store with about 1,000 products, frequent sales and substantial Google Shopping traffic, replies generally recommend compare-at pricing when a strikethrough must appear on product pages and in Google feeds. Native automatic discounts avoid changing product prices and suit short promotions, but may show only in the cart and often leave Google displaying the regular price.

Key safeguards for compare-at sales include exporting a pre-sale CSV, using a consistent process to restore prices, and limiting imports to price-related fields so stock or other changes are not overwritten. After a promotion, check for leftover compare-at prices, spot-check variants and review Merchant Center for price mismatches; Google updates may lag. Suggestions for tracking discount costs include recording per-product markdowns and checking sale prices against product costs.

Several replies also describe apps that schedule price changes, revert them or help review margins, though these are recommendations from their developers. No workflow was confirmed as adopted: the original build-versus-buy question and the store’s final choice remain unresolved.
